title: Thermochemistry and Thermodynamics
description: Energy changes in reactions, and the laws that decide which reactions go forward on their own.
overview: Every chemical reaction either releases energy to its surroundings or absorbs it. The burning of natural gas heats a house; the reaction in an instant cold pack cools your hand. Thermodynamics asks two questions about any change: how much energy is exchanged, and will it happen spontaneously?

This chapter defines energy, heat and work, introduces enthalpy and shows how to measure and calculate it. It then introduces entropy and the Gibbs free energy, which combine to predict spontaneity and, as the next chapter shows, the position of chemical equilibrium.
objectives: Apply the first law and the sign conventions for heat and work.
Distinguish enthalpy from internal energy and state functions from path functions.
Calculate heat with specific heat and calorimetry data.
Find ΔH° by Hess’s law, from enthalpies of formation, and from bond enthalpies.
Predict the sign of ΔS and compute ΔS° from tabulated entropies.
Use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS and ΔG° = −RT ln K to judge spontaneity and find equilibrium constants.

sections.title: Energy, heat and work
body: **Energy** is the capacity to do work or transfer heat. Its SI unit is the joule (1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻²); 1 cal = 4.184 J exactly. Energy of motion is **kinetic**, and stored energy, including chemical energy in bonds, is **potential**.

Thermodynamics divides the universe into the **system**, the part of interest (the reaction mixture), and the **surroundings**, everything else. An open system exchanges matter and energy with the surroundings, a closed system exchanges only energy, and an isolated system exchanges neither.

Energy crosses the boundary in two forms. **Heat** (q) is transfer due to a temperature difference. **Work** (w) is transfer by a force acting through a distance. For a gas expanding against constant external pressure, w = −PΔV. The **internal energy** U of a system is the sum of all kinetic and potential energies of its particles. The **first law** says that energy is conserved:

body.key: Sign convention: q and w are positive when energy flows into the system. A system that absorbs heat (q > 0) or has work done on it (w > 0, as when it is compressed) gains internal energy.

body: A process that releases heat to the surroundings is **exothermic** (q < 0); one that absorbs heat is **endothermic** (q > 0). Combustion and neutralization are exothermic. Melting ice and dissolving NH₄NO₃ in water are endothermic.

A **state function** depends only on the current state of the system, not on how it got there. U, H, S, G, P, V and T are state functions. Heat and work are **path functions**: climbing a mountain by two routes gives the same change in altitude (a state function) but different distances walked (a path function). ΔU for a reaction is fixed by the initial and final states, though q and w individually depend on how the reaction is carried out.

example.title: First law
example.problem: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work expanding. What is ΔU?
example.solution: q = +500 J. Work done by the system is negative: w = −200 J. ΔU = 500 − 200 = +300 J.

check.q: A system loses 150 J of heat and has 100 J of work done on it. What is ΔU?
Which of these is NOT a state function?

sections.title: Enthalpy and calorimetry
body: Most chemistry is done at constant pressure, open to the atmosphere. Then the heat exchanged is the change in **enthalpy**, H = U + PV:

ΔH < 0 for exothermic reactions and ΔH > 0 for endothermic ones. For reactions with no change in moles of gas, ΔH ≈ ΔU. A **thermochemical equation** pairs a balanced equation with its ΔH, for the amounts of moles written, with phases specified: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −571.6 kJ. Doubling the equation doubles ΔH, and reversing it changes its sign. The **standard state** is the pure substance at 1 bar, and ΔH° refers to reactants and products in their standard states at a stated temperature (usually 298.15 K).

The **heat capacity** C of an object is the heat needed to raise its temperature by 1 °C, C = q/ΔT. The **specific heat** c is per gram (J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹), and the **molar heat capacity** is per mole. Water’s is unusually large, 4.184 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, so water moderates climate and cools engines. Copper’s is 0.385, so a copper pan heats quickly.

**Calorimetry** measures heat by watching a temperature change. In a **coffee-cup calorimeter** (constant pressure) the heat released by the reaction is absorbed by the solution: q_rxn = −q_solution. In a **bomb calorimeter** a sample burns in a sealed steel vessel (constant volume), and q = C_cal ΔT gives ΔU.

example.title: Heat of neutralization
example.problem: 50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl and 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH, both at 21.0 °C, are mixed in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises to 27.5 °C. Find ΔH per mole of water formed. (Treat the solution as 100.0 g of water.)
solution: The accepted value is −55.8 kJ mol⁻¹; some heat is lost to the cup.

example.title: Bomb calorimeter
example.problem: Burning 1.500 g of glucose in a bomb calorimeter (C_cal = 10.5 kJ °C⁻¹) raises the temperature by 2.22 °C. Find ΔU of combustion per mole.

example.title: Heat exchange between objects
example.problem: 50.0 g of copper (c = 0.385) at 100.0 °C is dropped into 100.0 g of water at 20.0 °C. Find the final temperature.

check.q: How much heat is needed to warm 250 g of water by 10.0 °C?
For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, ΔH = −571.6 kJ. What is ΔH for H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O?

sections.title: Hess’s law and enthalpies of formation
body: Because H is a state function, the enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whether it takes place in one step or several. **Hess’s law** lets us add the equations of known reactions, and their ΔH values, to obtain an unmeasurable one.

example.title: Hess’s law
example.problem: Find ΔH° for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g), given (1) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH° = −393.5 kJ and (2) CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH° = −283.0 kJ.
solution: Keep equation (1) and reverse (2): CO₂ → CO + ½O₂, ΔH° = +283.0 kJ. Adding gives the target.

body: The **standard enthalpy of formation** ΔH_f° is the enthalpy change for forming one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states (C as graphite, O₂ as a gas). ΔH_f° of an element in its standard state is zero. Then any reaction’s enthalpy is

body.eq: ΔH°_{rxn} = Σ n ΔH_{f}°(products) − Σ n ΔH_{f}°(reactants)

example.title: Combustion of methane
example.problem: Find ΔH° for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), with ΔH_f° values in kJ mol⁻¹: CH₄ −74.8, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8.

body: Enthalpies of combustion are the heats released on burning fuels: natural gas, −890 kJ mol⁻¹ (−55.5 kJ g⁻¹); gasoline (octane), about −5470 kJ mol⁻¹ (−47.9 kJ g⁻¹); glucose, −2803 kJ mol⁻¹ (−15.6 kJ g⁻¹).

check.q: What is ΔH_f° for O₂(g) in its standard state?
If ΔH = −100 kJ for A → B, what is ΔH for 2B → 2A?

sections.title: Bond enthalpies
body: Breaking bonds costs energy and forming them releases it. For gas-phase reactions the enthalpy change can be estimated from average **bond enthalpies**:
These are averages over many compounds, so the estimates are accurate to only about 10%.

example.title: Estimating ΔH of combustion
example.problem: Estimate ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(g). Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O (in CO₂) 799, O–H 463.
solution: The actual value for water vapor is −802 kJ mol⁻¹.

check.q: H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 243, H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol. Estimate ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.

sections.title: Entropy and the second law
body: Energy conservation does not say which way a process goes. A hot cup cools in a cold room, never the reverse, though energy would be conserved either way. The missing criterion is **entropy**, S, which measures how many ways the energy and particles of a system can be arranged. Boltzmann’s formula is

where W is the number of **microstates** (microscopic arrangements) consistent with the observed macrostate. More ways means higher entropy. The **second law** states that the entropy of the universe increases in any spontaneous process: ΔS_univ = ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr > 0.

list: Gases have much higher entropy than liquids, which have higher entropy than solids. A reaction that produces gas, or more moles of gas, has ΔS > 0.
Entropy rises with temperature, with volume and with the number of particles. Dissolving a solid usually increases entropy.
More complex molecules, with more ways to store energy, have higher entropy.

body: The **third law** says that a perfect crystal at 0 K has S = 0. Absolute entropies can therefore be tabulated as **standard molar entropies** S°, always positive (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Then

body.eq: ΔS°_{rxn} = Σ n S°(products) − Σ n S°(reactants)

body: The surroundings gain entropy when they receive heat: ΔS_surr = −ΔH_sys/T at constant pressure and temperature. An exothermic reaction therefore increases the entropy of its surroundings, and this term is more important at low temperature.

example.title: Entropy change of ammonia synthesis
example.problem: Calculate ΔS° for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). S° (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹): N₂ 191.6, H₂ 130.7, NH₃ 192.8.
solution: The entropy falls because four moles of gas become two.

check.q: According to the third law, the entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is…
wrong: Equal to the entropy of the liquid

sections.title: Gibbs free energy and spontaneity
body: Checking ΔS for both system and surroundings is awkward. The **Gibbs free energy**, G = H − TS, packages the criterion in terms of the system alone. At constant temperature and pressure,

Since ΔS_univ = −ΔG/T, a process is **spontaneous** (it proceeds without outside intervention) if ΔG < 0, at equilibrium if ΔG = 0, and **nonspontaneous** if ΔG > 0. Spontaneous means “will go,” not “fast”: diamond turning to graphite is spontaneous but imperceptibly slow.

body: When ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, the changeover temperature is T = ΔH/ΔS. Ice melts above 273 K because ΔH and ΔS for melting are both positive: at 273.15 K, 6010 J mol⁻¹ / 273.15 K = 22.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ gives ΔG = 0.

Free energies of reaction are found from standard free energies of formation, ΔG°_rxn = ΣnΔG_f°(products) − ΣnΔG_f°(reactants), or from ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. The free energy is also the maximum non-expansion work a process can deliver: the electrical work from a battery is −ΔG.
Away from standard conditions, ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient. At equilibrium ΔG = 0 and Q = K, so
A negative ΔG° means K > 1, a positive ΔG° means K < 1, and every 5.7 kJ mol⁻¹ of ΔG° at 298 K changes K by a factor of 10.

example.title: Ammonia synthesis: free energy, K and temperature
example.problem: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, ΔH° = −91.8 kJ and ΔS° = −198.1 J K⁻¹. Find ΔG° and K at 298 K, and the temperature above which the reaction is no longer spontaneous under standard conditions.
solution: ΔH and ΔS are both negative, so the reaction is spontaneous only at low temperature. The crossover is T = ΔH/ΔS = 91,800/198.1 = 463 K. In industry a high temperature (700 K) is used anyway, to make the reaction fast enough, and high pressure compensates.

check.q: For a reaction with ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, spontaneity occurs…
ΔG° for a reaction is −20 kJ/mol at 298 K. K is…
Why does ice melt above 0 °C but freeze below?
check.a: ΔH and ΔS of melting are both positive, so TΔS outweighs ΔH above 273 K

summary: ΔU = q + w, with q and w positive for energy entering the system. U, H, S and G are state functions; q and w are not.
At constant pressure ΔH = q_p. q = mcΔT, and calorimetry measures heat from temperature changes.
Hess’s law: ΔH is path independent. ΔH° = ΣΔH_f°(products) − ΣΔH_f°(reactants). Bond enthalpies give estimates.
Entropy measures the number of microstates, S = k_B ln W. The entropy of the universe increases in spontaneous processes.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A reaction is spontaneous if ΔG < 0. ΔG° = −RT ln K links thermodynamics to equilibrium.

problems.q: Calculate ΔH° for 2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s) given ΔH_f° (kJ mol⁻¹): Al₂O₃ −1675.7, Fe₂O₃ −824.2. How much heat is released from 10.0 g of Al?
Given C(s) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ; H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), ΔH = −285.8 kJ; and C₂H₆ combustion: C₂H₆ + 7/2O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O(l), ΔH = −1560 kJ. Find ΔH_f° of ethane.
For the vaporization of water, ΔH° = +44.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +118.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 298 K. Find ΔG° at 298 K and the normal boiling point estimated from ΔH° and ΔS°.
problems.solution: ΔG° = 44.0 − 298(0.1188) = 8.6 kJ: nonspontaneous at 298 K (at 1 bar of vapor). Boiling point: T = ΔH/ΔS = 44,000/118.8 = 370 K.

problems.q: A reaction has K = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ at 298 K. Find ΔG°.
